parole

/puh-ROHL/ — rhymes with roll · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To parole someone is to release them from prison before their full sentence is served, on the condition that they follow certain rules while being supervised.

The board granted him parole after ten years of good behavior.

Example

After serving eight years of his fifteen-year sentence for theft, the prisoner was granted parole and released under strict supervision.

Parole is more specific than 'release' because it emphasizes conditional freedom — the person is released early from prison but must follow rules and is still monitored by authorities.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

release: Release is the general word for letting someone go — a fish, a hostage, a balloon — and it says nothing about conditions. Parole is a specific kind of release: let out of prison early, but supervised and bound by rules, with the sentence still hanging overhead.

amnesty: Amnesty is an official pardon that wipes an offense away, as if it had never happened — nothing is left to serve or supervise. Parole forgives nothing: the sentence still stands, and the person is simply allowed to finish it outside prison, under watch and under rules.

furlough: A furlough is a short, temporary permission to leave prison — a few days for a family funeral, say — after which the prisoner must come back and serve on. Parole is a lasting early release: the person leaves prison for good, so long as they follow the rules.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

imprisonment: being locked up to serve a sentence

detention: being held and kept from going free

Where it sits · how much liberty the person has — incarceration → parole → probation → freedom

incarceration vs. parole: Incarceration sits at the bottom of this freedom scale, well below parole: an incarcerated person is locked inside prison, while a person on parole has been let out early under supervision.

probation vs. parole: Probation allows a bit more freedom than parole — probation usually replaces prison time entirely, while parole is an early, supervised release from a sentence already being served behind bars.

freedom vs. parole: Freedom is the very top of this scale, beyond parole: a person on parole is out of prison but must still follow strict conditions, while true freedom comes with no conditions at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — parole

Root — parole: word, speech; a word of honor (French, from Late Latin parabola 'speech' (Greek parabole))

Put it together

Put it together: Parole is simply the French word for 'word' or 'speech' — a prisoner released early gives his word of honor to follow the rules, so being 'out on parole' literally means being out on your spoken promise.

Use the root in a new word: parliament

Use the root in a new word: parliament: A parliament is literally a 'place for talking' — it grew from the same French root parole, 'word or speech,' that names a released prisoner's word of honor.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / legal

Parole is the legal term for early release from prison with conditions and continued supervision. For general release from any situation, use 'release.' For a conditional sentence served in the community instead of prison, use 'probation.' Use parole specifically for early prison release.
